title: Government, Economy, and Technology in the Industrial Age
subject: AP World History

chunks.text: Historians divide industrialization into two phases. The first Industrial Revolution (c. 1750–1850) ran on coal, steam, iron, and textiles. The Second Industrial Revolution (c. 1850–1900) was built on a new, even more powerful cluster of technologies.

The Second Industrial Revolution (c. 1850–1900) was built on steel, electricity, chemicals, and the internal combustion engine. These technologies were even more productive than the coal-and-steam technologies of the first phase.

New processes such as the Bessemer process made it possible to mass-produce steel cheaply. Far stronger and more versatile than iron, steel made possible skyscrapers, longer bridges, better rails and machines, and powerful new weapons and warships.

The harnessing of electric power gave the world electric lighting, which extended the working and waking day, electric motors, and revolutionary communications, including the telegraph and later the telephone.

The telegraph let information travel almost instantly across continents and, via undersea cables, across oceans. It allowed a European capital to command and coordinate a colonial empire on the other side of the planet, tying communication technology to global power.

The chemical industry produced synthetic dyes, fertilizers, explosives, and new materials, transforming agriculture, manufacturing, and warfare. The internal combustion engine, burning petroleum, powered the automobile and eventually the airplane, making oil a strategic resource.

The Second Industrial Revolution deepened the gap between industrialized and non-industrialized regions and armed the industrial powers with steel warships, machine guns, and rapid communications that made the new wave of global imperialism militarily possible.

The corporation is a business owned by shareholders, many investors who buy shares (stock) and own a piece of the company. It could pool the capital of thousands of investors to fund massive projects far beyond what any individual or family could supply.

Limited liability meant a corporate investor could lose only the money they had invested, not their entire personal fortune, if the company failed. This made people far more willing to invest, unlocking capital for giant industrial projects.

Corporations raised capital by selling shares on stock markets (stock exchanges), where ownership stakes were bought and sold, and a sophisticated banking and finance sector grew up to channel money into industry. These institutions form the circulatory system of modern capitalism.

The drive for profit and scale produced monopolies, trusts, and cartels, in which a single company or alliance dominated an entire industry. By eliminating competition they could control prices and amass colossal wealth and power.

By the 1890s John D. Rockefeller's Standard Oil Company controlled roughly 90 percent of all oil refining in the United States, an organization richer and more powerful than many governments. Such concentrations eventually provoked antitrust laws and regulation.

Capitalism is the economic system in which the means of production (factories, land, capital) are privately owned and goods and prices are determined by free markets, by supply and demand, rather than by the state.

Laissez-faire (French for 'leave alone') is the principle, associated with Adam Smith's The Wealth of Nations (1776), that the economy works best when government interferes as little as possible, letting the 'invisible hand' of self-interested competition produce prosperity.

Early industrial Britain and the United States leaned heavily toward the free-market, minimal-government model, justifying leaving wages, working conditions, and prices to the market. No industrial economy, however, was ever purely laissez-faire.

Industrial-age free-trade liberalism was a sharp break from the older mercantilism of the previous era, which assumed tight state control of trade for national power. Liberalism argued instead for removing trade barriers and letting commerce flow freely.

Later industrializers like Japan (Meiji) and Russia used the state to drive industrialization directly, funding railroads, building industries, and protecting them with tariffs, because racing to catch up with powerful rivals required mobilizing resources fast.

Even in free-market Britain, the harsh realities of industrial life eventually forced governments to intervene with reforms: laws limiting working hours, banning child labor, improving public health, and later regulating monopolies. The trend over time was a gradual, contested expansion of government's role.

The role of government in industrial economies is best understood as a spectrum from laissez-faire (minimal government, free markets) to state-directed (the government funds, builds, and protects industry). Early industrializers leaned market-led; late industrializers leaned state-led.

The debate over government's role in the economy, from laissez-faire to state intervention, became one of the defining arguments of the modern world. It seeded the ideological battles between capitalism, socialism, and communism and shaped the politics of the entire twentieth century, including the Cold War.
